## The assignment

In class we built a house price model for Philadelphia. Now your team does it for a city you haven't modeled: **Chicago**.

The Cook County Assessor's Office has to value every home in the county, including the vast majority that didn't sell this year. Assessments drive property tax bills. When they're wrong in a systematic way, some households pay more than their share. A 2017 *Chicago Tribune* investigation, "The Tax Divide," found exactly that in Cook County: lower-value homes were assessed at higher shares of their worth than expensive ones.

Build a model that predicts **single-family sale prices in Chicago, 2023–2025**, using only the tools from this course. The file contains **only features of the house itself**. Everything about location is yours to build.

### A real test

| File | What's in it |
|---|---|
| `chicago_train.csv` | About 80% of the houses, **with** sale prices |
| `chicago_test.csv` | The other 20%, **without** sale prices. You predict them; we score you. |

The test houses were held out by house, not by sale, so a house that sold twice is entirely on one side. Your CV RMSE is your estimate. Your test RMSE is the truth. **If they're far apart, something leaked.**

**Due:** Friday, October 30. All teammates renders the file on their portfolio and every member submits that link on Canvas. One teammate uploads `team_XX_predictions.csv`.

**Individual accountability:** Q7 on October 30 asks each of you about *this* model: which features you used and why, your CV and test RMSE, and where the model fails worst. Make sure everyone can explain all of it.

### Rules

::: {.callout-important}
## 1. Clean training rows once, in Part 1. Never drop test rows.
You must predict every test house, so fill NAs in a feature rather than filtering.

## 2. Stay inside the time window
Open data from 2023–2025 only.

## 3. No leakage
Nothing built from sale prices. *Would the Assessor have this number for a house that didn't sell?*

## 4. The outcome stays in dollars
Transform predictors, not `sale_price`.

## 5. No prices from the test fold or the future
No features built from other houses' sale prices.
:::

### Please include in your final rendered qmd for this assignment:

| | |
|---|---|
| **Model log** | Every model you tried, in order, with CV RMSE and Moran's I. Each row has a note saying why you tried it. |
| **Features** | Incorporate the feature engineering tricks - including the spatial ones covered these past few weeks.
| **Diagnostics** | Residual maps for your baseline and final model, and what changed. |
| **Error analysis** | Where your final model fails worst, and whose homes it over-values (Part 4). |
| **Reasoning** | Choices justified by evidence from your own analysis.

## Part 0: Setup (provided)

Load the packages and set display options. Modeling functions are defined alongside their use in Part 2.

```{r}
#| label: setup
library(tidyverse)
library(tidycensus)
library(tigris)
library(sf)
library(spdep)
options(scipen = 999)
```

```{r}
#| label: formatting
money <- scales::label_dollar(accuracy = 1)
pct <- scales::label_percent(accuracy = 0.1)
theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 12))
dir.create("data/assignment5", recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
dir.create("reports/assignment5", recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
```

### Load both files together (provided)

Build every feature on `all_sales`, so training and test houses get identical features. Split off `train` again whenever you add something.

```{r}
#| label: load
raw_train <- read_csv("data/chicago_train.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
raw_test <- read_csv("data/chicago_test.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
stopifnot(!anyDuplicated(raw_train$id), !anyDuplicated(raw_test$id),
          length(intersect(raw_train$id, raw_test$id)) == 0)

all_sales <- bind_rows(
  raw_train %>% mutate(split = "train"),
  raw_test %>% mutate(split = "test")
) %>%
  st_as_sf(coords = c("lon", "lat"), crs = 4326, remove = FALSE) %>%
  st_transform(3435)            # Illinois East State Plane, feet

all_sales %>% st_drop_geometry() %>% count(split)
```

Useful sources: the [Chicago Data Portal](https://data.cityofchicago.org) (find a dataset's ID under its API button), the Census via `tidycensus`, and Cook County's open data.

## Part 1: Clean and explore

Decide which training sales are market sales. Record each rule, why, and how many it removed. Then explore: at least four plots, including a map of price.

```{r}
#| label: part-1
glimpse(all_sales)
all_sales %>% st_drop_geometry() %>% slice_head(n=6) %>% print(width = Inf)
```

```{r}
all_sales %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  count(split)
```

```{r}
all_sales %>% st_drop_geometry() %>% filter(split == "train") %>% summary()
```
### Inspect unusually small buildings
```{r}
all_sales %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  filter(split == "train") %>%
  select(id, sale_price, building_000sf, num_bedrooms,
         num_full_baths, lotsize_acre, building_age, is_multisale) %>%
  arrange(building_000sf) %>%
  slice_head(n = 10)
```
Some of the smallest buildings have room counts that seem high for their size. One record reports 246 square feet and a $700,000 sale price. We flagged it for further checking rather than removing it. We interpret `building_000sf` as thousands of square feet based on the column name, but the supplied files do not explain whether it includes basements or other structures.


```{r}
all_sales %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  filter(split == "train") %>%
  select(id, sale_price, building_000sf, num_bedrooms,
         num_full_baths, building_age, is_multisale) %>%
  arrange(desc(num_bedrooms), building_000sf) %>%
  slice_head(n = 10) %>%
  print(width = Inf)
```

The houses with the most bedrooms generally have larger building areas. But two pairs have matching values in this table and are flagged as multisales, so we looked more closely at those records.

```{r}
all_sales %>%
  filter(id %in% c(4348, 4349, 23563, 23564)) %>%
  mutate(
    location = st_as_text(geometry)
  ) %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  arrange(as.Date(sale_date, "%B %d, %Y"), id) %>%
  print(width = Inf)
```

These records share sale dates and prices, but their locations and some property attributes differ. They are not exact duplicates. Cook County uses `is_multisale` for transactions involving multiple parcels. A shared price does not tell us what each parcel sold for separately. We assume the course CSV uses the same definition. [Assessor's example](https://ccao-data-science---modeling.gitlab.io/packages/assessr/articles/finding-sales-comps.html), [official model documentation](https://github.com/ccao-data/model-res-avm#readme).

```{r}
all_sales %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  count(split, is_multisale) %>%
  group_by(split) %>%
  mutate(percent = round(100 * n / sum(n), 2))
```

We exclude the 1,232 training records flagged as multi-parcel sales (5.31%) because their prices may cover several parcels. That leaves 21,968 training observations. We keep every test record and do not set a minimum or maximum price cutoff. A very cheap or expensive sale is not necessarily an invalid one.


### Lowest unflagged prices
```{r}
all_sales %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  filter(split == "train", is_multisale == 0) %>%
  select(id, sale_date, sale_price, building_000sf,
         num_bedrooms, num_full_baths, building_age) %>%
  arrange(sale_price) %>%
  slice_head(n = 10) %>%
  print(width = Inf)
```



### Highest unflagged prices
```{r}
all_sales %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  filter(split == "train", is_multisale == 0) %>%
  select(id, sale_date, sale_price, building_000sf,
         num_bedrooms, num_full_baths, building_age) %>%
  arrange(desc(sale_price)) %>%
  slice_head(n = 10) %>%
  print(width = Inf)
```




### Apply the cleaning rules once

We exclude multi-parcel sales from training but retain every test house. We do not remove training sales solely because their prices are unusually low or high.

```{r}
#| label: clean-training
all_sales <- all_sales %>%
  mutate(
    sale_date = as.Date(sale_date, "%B %d, %Y"),
    property_group = paste(round(lon, 5), round(lat, 5)),
    eligible = split == "train" & is_multisale == 0 &
      is.finite(sale_price) & sale_price > 0
  )
stopifnot(!anyNA(all_sales$sale_date), all(all_sales$year %in% 2023:2025))

train_single <- all_sales %>%
  filter(split == "train", is_multisale == 0)
if (interactive()) View(train_single)
glimpse(train_single)

train <- train_single %>%
  filter(is.finite(sale_price), sale_price > 0)
if (interactive()) View(train)
glimpse(train)


cleaning_log <- tibble(
  stage = c("Original training rows", "Exclude multi-parcel sales",
            "Exclude missing/nonpositive prices"),
  remaining = c(nrow(raw_train), nrow(train_single), nrow(train))
) %>%
  mutate(removed_at_step = lag(remaining, default = first(remaining)) - remaining)
if (interactive()) View(cleaning_log)
glimpse(cleaning_log)

missing_log <- all_sales %>% st_drop_geometry() %>% select(-property_group, -eligible) %>%
  group_by(split) %>% summarise(across(everything(), ~ sum(is.na(.x)))) %>%
  pivot_longer(-split, names_to = "variable", values_to = "missing") %>%
  filter(missing > 0)
if (interactive()) View(missing_log)
glimpse(missing_log)

test <- all_sales %>% filter(split == "test")
stopifnot(nrow(test) == nrow(raw_test))

```

We fill the six predictors that have missing values with medians from the fitting rows. During cross-validation, we calculate those medians separately inside each fitting fold. We use the same medians to fill that fold's held-out rows. We do not add missingness indicators or fill in test sale prices.

### Exploration plots

We use the cleaned training data to see how prices relate to size, age and location. These plots help us choose what to test in the models. We then use cross-validation to see whether those choices help.

We start by looking at the price distribution. We want to see where most sales fall and how far the highest prices are from the rest. Errors on those expensive houses can have a big effect on RMSE. The labels are in millions, so `$1m` means $1,000,000. We are only changing the labels, not the prices.

```{r}
#| label: price-histogram
#| fig-cap: "Prices are right-skewed. The dollar-axis histogram retains every cleaned training sale."
ggplot(st_drop_geometry(train), aes(sale_price)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 60, fill = "#287D8E", color = "white") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::label_dollar(scale = 1e-6, suffix = "m")) +
  labs(x = "Sale price", y = "Sales")
```

Next, we compare building size with price. Do bigger houses sell for more, and how much do prices vary for houses of the same size? We multiply `building_000sf` by 1,000 to show square feet. The log axes make the smaller values easier to see alongside the larger ones, and transparency helps when points overlap. Our model still predicts prices in dollars. If the relationship looks curved, we have a reason to test a size transformation.

```{r}
#| label: price-size
#| fig-cap: "Building size and price; both display axes are logarithmic. The regression outcome remains dollars."
ggplot(st_drop_geometry(train), aes(building_000sf * 1000, sale_price)) +
  geom_point(alpha = .15, size = .6, color = "#287D8E") +
  scale_x_log10(labels = scales::label_comma()) + scale_y_log10(labels = money) +
  labs(x = "Reported building area (square feet)", y = "Sale price (log display)")
```

We also look at price against building age. We want to see whether a straight-line relationship seems reasonable or whether we should test age squared as well. We do not remove a house just because it is old. Again, the log price axis is only for the plot.

```{r}
#| label: age-price
#| fig-cap: "Prices vary widely within building ages; age alone is not a cleaning rule."
ggplot(st_drop_geometry(train), aes(building_age, sale_price)) +
  geom_point(alpha = .12, size = .6, color = "#287D8E") +
  scale_y_log10(labels = money) + labs(x = "Building age (years)", y = "Sale price (log display)")
```

Finally, we map the sales to see where higher and lower prices cluster. Each point is a sale, and the color shows its price. If prices vary across the city, we have a reason to test location features alongside house characteristics. The map alone cannot explain why those differences exist. We use a log color scale so a few expensive sales do not dominate the colors.

```{r}
#| label: training-price-map
#| fig-cap: "Cleaned training sales. Color uses a logarithmic price scale; no expensive records are hidden."
#| fig-height: 7
ggplot(train) + geom_sf(aes(color = sale_price), size = .35, alpha = .6) +
  scale_color_viridis_c(trans = "log10", labels = money, name = "Sale price") +
  coord_sf(datum = NA) + labs(x = NULL, y = NULL)
```

**Answer: What in your exploration shaped your modeling choices?**

Houses with similar sizes sell for very different prices, so we did not expect house characteristics alone to explain everything. We started with a structure-only model, then tested squared size and age terms and an alternative using log size. The map also gave us a reason to test location features. We used cross-validation to check whether those additions helped.

We kept the unusually low and high prices because we did not have enough evidence to call them errors. That choice has consequences: expensive sales can drive dollar RMSE, while a relatively small dollar error can be a large percentage of a cheap house's price. We return to both issues in Part 4.

## Part 2: Build the model

Start with a structure-only baseline. Then add features in steps you can learn from, logging each one. Keep the log in a tibble with columns `model`, `added`, `cv_rmse`, `moran_i`, `notes`.

### Download the 2023 geographic and income data

We use 2023 Census tract boundaries and ACS income estimates. The code downloads them if they are not already saved locally. We reuse those source files, but rerun the analysis when rendering the document. The Census key stays in the local configuration.

```{r}
#| label: download-sources
options(timeout = 240, tigris_use_cache = TRUE)
income_file <- "data/assignment5/acs_income_2023.rds"
tract_file <- "data/assignment5/cook_tracts_2023.rds"

# These caches contain downloaded source data only, never fitted models or results.
if (!file.exists(income_file)) {
  income_source <- get_acs(
    geography = "tract", variables = "B19013_001", state = "IL",
    county = "Cook", year = 2023, survey = "acs5", geometry = FALSE
  )
  stopifnot(nrow(income_source) > 1000)
  saveRDS(income_source, income_file)
}
if (!file.exists(tract_file)) {
  tract_source <- tigris::tracts(
    state = "IL", county = "Cook", year = 2023, cb = TRUE,
    progress_bar = FALSE
  ) %>% st_transform(3435)
  stopifnot(nrow(tract_source) > 1000)
  saveRDS(tract_source, tract_file)
}

income <- readRDS(income_file) %>%
  transmute(GEOID, income = if_else(estimate > 0, estimate, NA_real_), income_moe = moe)
tracts <- readRDS(tract_file) %>% select(GEOID, NAME)
```

### Build the location features

We join each house to its Census tract for the income comparison later. We also calculate distance from the Loop and make three distance rings. These use the same spatial joins, distance calculations and `case_when()` patterns as the notes.

```{r}
#| label: spatial-features
all_sales <- st_join(
  all_sales, tracts %>% select(tract = GEOID),
  join = st_intersects, left = TRUE
) %>%
  distinct(id, .keep_all = TRUE) %>%
  left_join(income, by = c("tract" = "GEOID"))

stopifnot(nrow(all_sales) == nrow(raw_train) + nrow(raw_test))

cbd <- st_sfc(st_point(c(-87.6298, 41.8781)), crs = 4326) %>%
  st_transform(3435)

all_sales$dist_cbd_mi <- as.numeric(st_distance(all_sales, cbd)) / 5280

all_sales <- all_sales %>%
  mutate(
    ring = case_when(
      dist_cbd_mi < 3 ~ "Core",
      dist_cbd_mi < 8 ~ "Inner",
      TRUE ~ "Outer"
    ),
    ring = factor(ring, levels = c("Core", "Inner", "Outer")),
    year_f = factor(year),
    quarter_f = factor(sale_qrt)
  )

# Label 2-mile squares using projected coordinates.
xy <- st_coordinates(all_sales)
origin <- st_coordinates(cbd)[1, ]
all_sales$grid_raw <- paste(
  floor((xy[, 1] - origin[1]) / (2 * 5280)),
  floor((xy[, 2] - origin[2]) / (2 * 5280)),
  sep = ":"
)

train <- all_sales %>% filter(eligible)
test <- all_sales %>% filter(split == "test")
```


The grid label is a place category, like the district factor in Week 6. Dividing coordinates by the width of a 2-mile square and rounding down with `floor()` puts houses into cells. The cells are a modeling choice, not official neighborhoods. They use no price information.

### Set aside the audit sample

We keep records with the same rounded location together. We use 80% of these groups to compare models and reserve the rest for an audit. We keep this split fixed throughout.

```{r}
#| label: validation-split
set.seed(5080)
groups <- sample(unique(train$property_group))
audit_groups <- groups[seq_len(ceiling(length(groups) * 0.2))]

development <- train %>% filter(!property_group %in% audit_groups)

# Count distinct location groups, rather than repeated sales, in each cell.
large_grids <- development %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  distinct(grid_raw, property_group) %>%
  count(grid_raw) %>%
  filter(n >= 15) %>%
  pull(grid_raw)

all_sales <- all_sales %>%
  mutate(
    grid_fe = if_else(grid_raw %in% large_grids, grid_raw, "Other"),
    grid_fe = factor(grid_fe)
  )

train <- all_sales %>% filter(eligible)
test <- all_sales %>% filter(split == "test")
development <- train %>% filter(!property_group %in% audit_groups)
audit <- train %>% filter(property_group %in% audit_groups)

tibble(
  sample = c("Development", "Audit", "Test"),
  rows = c(nrow(development), nrow(audit), nrow(test))
)
```


We pool small grid categories as "Other" so we are less likely to hold out a category with no fitting examples. As the notes explain, a minimum count is a precaution, not a guarantee. We check factor coverage below. Rounded coordinates are only a proxy for property IDs, and nearby houses can still appear across folds.

### Fill missing predictors

The assignment requires a prediction for every test house. We therefore fill missing predictors instead of dropping test rows. This function uses `mutate()`, `replace_na()` and `median()` explicitly, one column at a time. The `reference` argument tells us which fitting rows provide the medians.

```{r}
#| label: fill-missing
fill_missing <- function(data, reference) {
  data <- st_drop_geometry(data)
  reference <- st_drop_geometry(reference)

  data %>%
    mutate(
      lotsize_acre = replace_na(lotsize_acre,
        median(reference$lotsize_acre, na.rm = TRUE)),
      num_half_baths = replace_na(num_half_baths,
        median(reference$num_half_baths, na.rm = TRUE)),
      num_fireplaces = replace_na(num_fireplaces,
        median(reference$num_fireplaces, na.rm = TRUE)),
      garage_size = replace_na(garage_size,
        median(reference$garage_size, na.rm = TRUE)),
      full_basement = replace_na(full_basement,
        median(reference$full_basement, na.rm = TRUE)),
      warmairfurnace = replace_na(warmairfurnace,
        median(reference$warmairfurnace, na.rm = TRUE))
    )
}
```


### Create the same folds for every model

This follows Week 7's grouped-fold lookup. All sales in one location group receive the same fold number.

```{r}
#| label: prepare-folds
development_data <- development %>% st_drop_geometry()
unique_properties <- unique(development_data$property_group)

set.seed(5080)
property_folds <- sample(rep(1:10, length.out = length(unique_properties)))
folds <- property_folds[match(development_data$property_group, unique_properties)]

table(folds)

# Week 6's check for categories missing from a fitting fold.
coverage_check <- map_dfr(1:10, function(k) {
  map_dfr(c("ring", "grid_fe", "year_f", "quarter_f"), function(v) {
    fitting_levels <- unique(as.character(development_data[[v]][folds != k]))
    validation_levels <- unique(as.character(development_data[[v]][folds == k]))
    tibble(
      fold = k,
      variable = v,
      unseen_levels = paste(setdiff(validation_levels, fitting_levels), collapse = ", ")
    )
  })
})

if (any(coverage_check$unseen_levels != "")) {
  stop("A validation category is absent from fitting rows.")
}
```


### Write the model formulas

We compare eight formulas in steps: house attributes, squared terms and timing, log size, distance, distance squared, rings, an interaction, and grid fixed effects. The outcome stays in dollars. `log(1 + lotsize_acre)` expresses the earlier log-lot transformation using ordinary arithmetic.

```{r}
#| label: candidate-formulas
f0 <- sale_price ~ building_000sf + building_age + lotsize_acre + num_bedrooms +
  num_full_baths + num_half_baths + num_fireplaces + garage_size + central_air +
  one_story + full_basement + finished_basement + brick_stone_ext + warmairfurnace

f1 <- sale_price ~ building_000sf + building_age + num_bedrooms + num_full_baths +
  num_half_baths + num_fireplaces + garage_size + central_air + one_story +
  full_basement + finished_basement + brick_stone_ext + warmairfurnace +
  log(1 + lotsize_acre) + I(building_000sf^2) + I(building_age^2) + year_f +
  quarter_f

f2 <- sale_price ~ building_age + num_bedrooms + num_full_baths + num_half_baths +
  num_fireplaces + garage_size + central_air + one_story + full_basement +
  finished_basement + brick_stone_ext + warmairfurnace + log(1 + lotsize_acre) +
  I(building_age^2) + year_f + quarter_f + log(building_000sf)

f3 <- sale_price ~ building_000sf + building_age + num_bedrooms + num_full_baths +
  num_half_baths + num_fireplaces + garage_size + central_air + one_story +
  full_basement + finished_basement + brick_stone_ext + warmairfurnace +
  log(1 + lotsize_acre) + I(building_000sf^2) + I(building_age^2) + year_f +
  quarter_f + dist_cbd_mi

f4 <- sale_price ~ building_000sf + building_age + num_bedrooms + num_full_baths +
  num_half_baths + num_fireplaces + garage_size + central_air + one_story +
  full_basement + finished_basement + brick_stone_ext + warmairfurnace +
  log(1 + lotsize_acre) + I(building_000sf^2) + I(building_age^2) + year_f +
  quarter_f + dist_cbd_mi + I(dist_cbd_mi^2)

f5 <- sale_price ~ building_000sf + building_age + num_bedrooms + num_full_baths +
  num_half_baths + num_fireplaces + garage_size + central_air + one_story +
  full_basement + finished_basement + brick_stone_ext + warmairfurnace +
  log(1 + lotsize_acre) + I(building_000sf^2) + I(building_age^2) + year_f +
  quarter_f + ring

f6 <- sale_price ~ building_000sf + building_age + num_bedrooms + num_full_baths +
  num_half_baths + num_fireplaces + garage_size + central_air + one_story +
  full_basement + finished_basement + brick_stone_ext + warmairfurnace +
  log(1 + lotsize_acre) + I(building_000sf^2) + I(building_age^2) + year_f +
  quarter_f + ring + building_000sf:ring

f7 <- sale_price ~ building_000sf + building_age + num_bedrooms + num_full_baths +
  num_half_baths + num_fireplaces + garage_size + central_air + one_story +
  full_basement + finished_basement + brick_stone_ext + warmairfurnace +
  log(1 + lotsize_acre) + I(building_000sf^2) + I(building_age^2) + year_f +
  quarter_f + grid_fe + ring + building_000sf:ring

formulas <- list(
  House_only = f0,
  Curved_and_time = f1,
  Log_size = f2,
  Downtown_distance = f3,
  Squared_distance = f4,
  Distance_rings = f5,
  Size_by_ring = f6,
  Grid_effects = f7
)
```


### Cross-validation and spatial weights

The prediction loop follows Week 7. The only extra preparation is filling missing values from the fitting fold before calling `lm()`. We retain the earlier rule that negative predictions become zero, written as a direct replacement. This is an output constraint, not a rule for removing training houses.

```{r}
#| label: validation-functions
cv_predictions <- function(formula, data, fold_id) {
  stopifnot(nrow(data) == length(fold_id), !anyNA(fold_id))
  predictions <- rep(NA_real_, nrow(data))

  for (k in sort(unique(fold_id))) {
    validation <- fold_id == k

    fitting <- fill_missing(data[!validation, ], data[!validation, ])
    validating <- fill_missing(data[validation, ], data[!validation, ])

    fit <- lm(formula, data = fitting, na.action = na.fail)
    predictions[validation] <- predict(fit, newdata = validating)
  }

  stopifnot(all(is.finite(predictions)))
  predictions[predictions < 0] <- 0
  predictions
}

morans_i <- function(values, weights) {
  moran(values, weights, n = length(values), S0 = Szero(weights))$I
}

coords <- st_coordinates(development)
has_duplicate_locations <- anyDuplicated(coords) > 0
house_knn <- knearneigh(
  coords, k = 5, longlat = FALSE,
  use_kd_tree = !has_duplicate_locations
)
house_nb <- knn2nb(house_knn)
weights <- nb2listw(house_nb, style = "W")
```


We use five nearest neighbors and row-standardized weights, as in Week 7. We do not shift coordinates or symmetrize the graph. Duplicate locations can create ties, so their ordering can affect the neighbor choice.

### Compare the models

We use Week 7's `lapply()` pattern to apply the same CV function to each named formula. `imap_dfr()` then puts those results into one table. Every model uses the same rows, folds and dollar units.

```{r}
#| label: part-2
evaluations <- lapply(formulas, function(f) {
  predictions <- cv_predictions(f, development_data, folds)
  errors <- development_data$sale_price - predictions
  list(
    predictions = predictions,
    cv_rmse = sqrt(mean(errors^2)),
    moran_i = morans_i(errors, weights)
  )
})

model_log <- imap_dfr(evaluations, function(result, model_name) {
  tibble(
    model = model_name,
    cv_rmse = result$cv_rmse,
    moran_i = result$moran_i
  )
}) %>%
  mutate(
    added = c("House characteristics only",
      "Squared size/age, log lot area, year and quarter",
      "Log size instead of quadratic size",
      "Add distance to the Loop",
      "Add squared distance",
      "Use distance rings",
      "Let the size slope vary by ring",
      "Add 2-mile geographic fixed effects"),
    notes = "Same grouped folds; median filling inside fitting folds; negative outputs set to zero"
  ) %>%
  select(model, added, cv_rmse, moran_i, notes)

knitr::kable(model_log, digits = 3,
             caption = "Current comparison: eight course-style formulas")
```


We removed missingness indicators and the coordinate-surface experiments to keep the current workflow focused on the notes' patterns. Earlier trials are retained separately below rather than mixed into this comparison. Because preprocessing, fold assignment and the spatial weights now follow the simpler setup, we recalculate all scores instead of reusing earlier numbers. The experimental grid-by-size model from the separate review has not been added.

The audit contains `r nrow(audit)` sales and has already been inspected in earlier work. We use it as an additional diagnostic, not an untouched final test. ## Part 3: Final model

Show your final model, the model log, and baseline vs. final residual maps.

### Choose a formula and check the audit sample

We choose the smallest development CV RMSE. The named formula list lets us select the corresponding formula with `[[best_name]]`. We then fit it to the development rows and predict the audit rows.

```{r}
#| label: select-and-audit
best_row <- model_log %>% arrange(cv_rmse) %>% slice_head(n = 1)
best_name <- best_row$model
f_final <- formulas[[best_name]]

development_filled <- fill_missing(development, development)
audit_filled <- fill_missing(audit, development)

baseline_fit <- lm(f0, data = development_filled, na.action = na.fail)
selected_fit <- lm(f_final, data = development_filled, na.action = na.fail)

audit_baseline <- predict(baseline_fit, newdata = audit_filled)
audit_pred <- predict(selected_fit, newdata = audit_filled)
audit_baseline[audit_baseline < 0] <- 0
audit_pred[audit_pred < 0] <- 0
stopifnot(all(is.finite(audit_pred)))

audit_scores <- tibble(
  model = c("House_only", best_name),
  rmse = c(
    sqrt(mean((audit$sale_price - audit_baseline)^2)),
    sqrt(mean((audit$sale_price - audit_pred)^2))
  ),
  mae = c(
    mean(abs(audit$sale_price - audit_baseline)),
    mean(abs(audit$sale_price - audit_pred))
  )
)

audit <- audit %>%
  mutate(pred = audit_pred, residual = sale_price - pred,
         abs_error = abs(residual), ratio = pred / sale_price)
```


### Fit the final model on all cleaned training rows

We use grouped folds again to report the selected formula's CV error across all cleaned training rows. Then we fit one final model to those rows. Test predictors are filled using training medians.

```{r}
#| label: final-fit
train_data <- train %>% st_drop_geometry()
unique_properties <- unique(train_data$property_group)
set.seed(5080)
property_folds <- sample(rep(1:10, length.out = length(unique_properties)))
full_folds <- property_folds[match(train_data$property_group, unique_properties)]

full_predictions <- cv_predictions(f_final, train_data, full_folds)
final_cv_rmse <- sqrt(mean((train_data$sale_price - full_predictions)^2))

final_training <- fill_missing(train, train)
final_test <- fill_missing(test, train)
m_final <- lm(f_final, data = final_training, na.action = na.fail)
```


```{r}
#| label: part-3
best_row <- model_log %>% filter(model == best_name)
baseline_row <- model_log %>% filter(model == "House_only")
best_name
f_final
knitr::kable(audit_scores %>% mutate(across(c(rmse, mae), money)),
             caption = "Separate audit subset; not used to rank the candidate formulas")
summary(m_final)
```

```{r}
#| label: residual-comparison
#| fig-height: 7
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-cap: "Actual minus out-of-fold prediction on the identical development sample. Positive means underprediction. Colors saturate at the common 95th percentile of absolute errors; all points remain shown."
residual_maps <- bind_rows(
  development %>% mutate(model = "Structure-only baseline",
    residual = sale_price - evaluations[["House_only"]]$predictions),
  development %>% mutate(model = "Selected model",
    residual = sale_price - evaluations[[best_name]]$predictions))
limit <- as.numeric(quantile(abs(residual_maps$residual), .95))
ggplot(residual_maps) + geom_sf(aes(color = residual), size = .3, alpha = .65) +
  facet_wrap(~model) + coord_sf(datum = NA) +
  scale_color_gradient2(low = "#2166AC", mid = "#F7F7F7", high = "#B2182B",
    limits = c(-limit, limit), oob = scales::squish, labels = money,
    name = "Residual ($)") + labs(x = NULL, y = NULL)
```

**Answer: What helped most, and what disappointed you?**

We chose `r best_name` because it had the lowest development CV RMSE: `r money(best_row$cv_rmse)`, compared with `r money(baseline_row$cv_rmse)` for the baseline. That's a `r pct(1 - best_row$cv_rmse / baseline_row$cv_rmse)` reduction. The model log shows which additions helped under the same validation setup. We use that evidence rather than choosing the most complicated formula.

We compared log size, squared terms and several ways to include location. Residual Moran's I changed from `r round(baseline_row$moran_i, 3)` to `r round(best_row$moran_i, 3)`, but some spatial pattern remained. The model with the lowest RMSE did not necessarily have the lowest Moran's I.

On the audit sample, RMSE was `r money(audit_scores$rmse[2])`, compared with `r money(audit_scores$rmse[1])` for the baseline. That supports the improvement on separate records. This is the best of the candidates we tested, not the best possible model. This audit has already been inspected during earlier work, so it is not a fresh independent test.

## Part 4: Where it fails, and who pays

**4A.** Where does your final model fail worst? Is it guessing too high or too low there, and why do you think so?

**4B.** Assessors judge their work with the **ratio** of predicted value to sale price. A ratio above 1 means the home is over-valued and its owner over-taxed. Does your model's ratio differ by neighborhood income? Connect your answer to your Part 1 cleaning rules and to "The Tax Divide."

```{r}
#| label: error-diagnostics
# Retrospective income context is deliberately excluded from all model formulas.
cuts <- quantile(income$income[is.finite(income$income)], c(1/3, 2/3), names = FALSE)
audit <- audit %>% mutate(income_group = factor(case_when(
  is.na(income) ~ "Unknown", income <= cuts[1] ~ "Lower", income <= cuts[2] ~ "Middle", TRUE ~ "Higher"),
  levels = c("Lower", "Middle", "Higher", "Unknown")))
fairness <- audit %>% st_drop_geometry() %>% group_by(income_group) %>% summarise(
  n = n(), median_income = median(income, na.rm = TRUE), median_ratio = median(ratio),
  aggregate_ratio = sum(pred) / sum(sale_price), share_overvalued = mean(ratio > 1),
  mae = mean(abs_error), .groups = "drop")
price_fairness <- audit %>% st_drop_geometry() %>%
  mutate(price_group = ntile(sale_price, 4)) %>% group_by(price_group) %>% summarise(
    n = n(), median_price = median(sale_price), median_ratio = median(ratio), .groups = "drop")
geographic_errors <- audit %>% st_drop_geometry() %>% group_by(tract) %>% summarise(
  n = n(), mae = mean(abs_error), mean_residual = mean(residual), .groups = "drop") %>%
  filter(n >= 10) %>% arrange(desc(mae))
worst <- audit %>% st_drop_geometry() %>% arrange(desc(abs_error)) %>%
  select(id, tract, sale_price, pred, residual, building_000sf, income_group) %>% slice_head(n = 10)
income_cuts <- cuts
audit_coords <- st_coordinates(audit)
audit_has_duplicates <- anyDuplicated(audit_coords) > 0
audit_knn <- knearneigh(
  audit_coords, k = 5, longlat = FALSE,
  use_kd_tree = !audit_has_duplicates
)
audit_nb <- knn2nb(audit_knn)
audit_weights <- nb2listw(audit_nb, style = "W")
audit_moran <- morans_i(audit$residual, audit_weights)
validation <- list(unmatched_tracts = sum(is.na(all_sales$tract)))
```

```{r}
#| label: part-4
knitr::kable(worst %>% mutate(across(c(sale_price, pred, residual), money)),
             caption = "Largest absolute errors in the audit subset")
knitr::kable(head(geographic_errors, 10) %>% mutate(across(c(mae, mean_residual), money)),
             caption = "Highest audit MAE by tract, restricted to at least 10 audit sales")
knitr::kable(fairness %>% mutate(median_income = money(median_income),
  across(c(median_ratio, aggregate_ratio), ~ round(.x, 3)),
  share_overvalued = pct(share_overvalued), mae = money(mae)),
  caption = "Audit valuation ratios by tract-income group; counts are sales, not residents")
knitr::kable(price_fairness %>% mutate(median_price = money(median_price),
  median_ratio = round(median_ratio, 3)), caption = "Additional audit check by observed-price quartile")
```

```{r}
#| label: income-ratios
#| fig-cap: "Median predicted/observed price ratios in the audit subset. A ratio above 1 indicates overprediction, not a directly calculated tax bill."
ggplot(filter(fairness, income_group != "Unknown"), aes(income_group, median_ratio)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#287D8E", width = .65) + geom_hline(yintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(median_ratio, 2)), vjust = -.4) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, .12))) +
  labs(x = "Tract median-household-income group", y = "Median valuation ratio")
```

**4A.** We compared tracts with at least 10 audit sales. Tract `r geographic_errors$tract[1]` had the highest MAE at `r money(geographic_errors$mae[1])`. Its mean residual was `r money(geographic_errors$mean_residual[1])`, so our predictions were `r ifelse(geographic_errors$mean_residual[1] > 0, "too low on average", "too high on average")` there.

Our largest individual error was record `r worst$id[1]`: it sold for `r money(worst$sale_price[1])`, but we predicted `r money(worst$pred[1])`. Differences between luxury houses, missing condition information and inaccurate area measurements could contribute to these errors. We cannot tell which explanation applies from these columns alone. Audit residual Moran's I was `r round(audit_moran, 3)`, so spatial errors remain. Holding out entire areas or a later year could also give worse results than these random grouped splits.

**4B.** We split county tracts into three income groups using cutoffs of `r money(income_cuts[1])` and `r money(income_cuts[2])`. The lower-income group's median predicted-to-sale-price ratio was `r round(fairness$median_ratio[fairness$income_group == "Lower"], 3)`, compared with `r round(fairness$median_ratio[fairness$income_group == "Higher"], 3)` for the higher-income group. We also report group sizes, the share overpredicted and the ratio of summed predictions to summed prices. That last measure gives more weight to expensive sales, so it can differ from the median individual ratio.

The larger warning is in the lowest-price quartile. Its median ratio was `r round(price_fairness$median_ratio[1], 3)`, about `r pct(price_fairness$median_ratio[1] - 1)` overprediction. Lower dollar RMSE clearly does not guarantee small percentage errors for inexpensive houses. Grouping houses by their observed prices can also produce regression-to-the-mean patterns, so this comparison alone does not prove discrimination.

We kept cheap sales rather than excluding them just because they were hard to predict. Removing bundled sales made the training prices easier to interpret, but our audit results do not tell us how well the model handles the flagged test transactions. The *Tax Divide* investigation gives us a reason to take these proportional errors seriously. We are measuring prediction errors here, not calculating tax bills or estimating a causal effect of income. [The Tax Divide investigation](https://apps.chicagotribune.com/news/watchdog/cook-county-property-tax-divide/).

Tract income is not an owner's income, and ACS estimates have sampling uncertainty. Across all input rows, `r validation$unmatched_tracts` had no tract match. We left those unmatched and did not borrow income from a nearby tract.

Our final grouped 10-fold CV RMSE on all cleaned training sales is `r money(final_cv_rmse)`. We calculated it after choosing the model, so it is a post-selection check. The separate audit RMSE is `r money(audit_scores$rmse[2])`. We will only know the instructor's test RMSE after scoring.

We save the predictions to `reports/assignment5/team_XX_predictions.csv`, with all `r nrow(preds)` test IDs in their original order. We still need to replace `XX` with our team number before uploading. The zero bound affects `r sum(preds$pred == 0)` predictions. Those houses need review: zero is a sign that the model has failed for those records, not a believable house value. We do not cap high predictions or add a positive price floor.

## Part 6: Reflection (about 300 words, as a team)

1. **Read one coefficient twice:** once as β̂, once for what it does to ŷ.
2. **Would you hand this model to the Assessor?** What would you warn them about?

We started with house characteristics and added location features because similar houses can sell for different prices across Chicago. We tested place-specific intercepts and an interaction that lets the size slope change with distance from the Loop. We chose among these formulas using development CV. The fitted relationships do not tell us what changing a house or its surroundings would cause.

Our `central_air` coefficient is `r money(unname(coef(m_final)["central_air"]))`. As beta-hat, it is the estimated price difference between the two central-air categories, holding the other predictors fixed. For y-hat, switching the indicator from 0 to 1 changes the raw predicted price by that amount. Near zero, the output bound can change the size of that difference. We cannot interpret this as the return from installing air conditioning because condition and renovations may also differ between houses.

We would not give this model to the Assessor for operational use yet. It improves on the baseline, but the lowest-price audit quartile is still substantially overpredicted. Expensive sales also have a large influence on dollar RMSE. A better overall score does not settle the fairness question, and tract income cannot tell us whether each owner's assessment is fair.

We removed bundled transactions rather than guessing how their prices should be divided. We kept both price tails because we could not justify excluding them. Grouping rounded coordinates helps with repeat sales, but verified parcel IDs would be better. Before using the model for assessments, we would test it on a later year and on held-out geographic areas, check property condition and transaction details, and estimate prediction uncertainty. The zero-valued test predictions also need individual review. They show where the model breaks down, not houses that should be assessed at zero.
